catalog_locator: sec. 2.3.1 'Stress', pp. 24-29 (page number printed at the top of each page); restated p. 9 (ch. 1 overview), p. 17 (long vowels), p. 18 (diphthongs), the ch. 2 summary p. 36 and sec. 11.1.2
catalog_quote: p. 24: "The primary stress in Adang falls on the final syllable. I shall briefly illustrate this, starting from stress on monosyllabic monomorphemic words to polysyllabic poly morphemic and compound words; and words in sentential contexts. Note that a word in Adang is composed of an obligatory root (i.e. a free morpheme), optionally prefixed by pronominals (see for details in 3) and/ or cliticized by aspectual enclitics (see for details in 4.5)." p. 25: "As can be seen from the list, the primary stress is on the final syllable of each of the words." p. 26: "From the list observe that the primary stress falls on the final syllable of every word in (8) and (9. a) but in (9. b), the primary stress does not fall on the final syllable, namely on the morphemes -eh and -am. ... So they cliticize to a word, and stress is assigned within the word, excluding clitics." p. 28: "Thus, the different position of the primary stress in (12-14) distinguish different types of utterances (words, phrases, idioms serial verbs and clauses), but does not distinguish one word from another." p. 29: "To summarize, primary stress in Adang falls on the final syllable of a word. In a compound noun, phrase or idiom and serial verb, the primary stress is assigned to the final syllable of the first word."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for Adang, so there is nothing to agree with or contradict; this is the first first-hand statement and supplies a new fixed: final syllable entry with the clitic exclusion and the first-word rule for compounds/phrases. It is consistent with the family-level remark in Holton & Robinson (Klamer ed. 2017, p. 55) that most Alor-Pantar languages have penultimate stress only in the sense that Adang is one of the exceptions they leave unnamed; Haan's final-syllable statement is Adang-specific and should take precedence for this language.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the last syllable of the word (root plus pronominal prefixes); the aspectual enclitics -eh (PROG) and -am (PERF) stand outside the stress domain, so stress stays on the last syllable of the host. In compounds, two-word phrases, idioms and serial-verb constructions only the first word carries primary stress (on its final syllable). Stress does not distinguish one word from another; it distinguishes utterance types (word vs phrase vs clause). In phonetically long vowels and rising diphthongs the stress sits on the second/final vocalic element, which Haan uses to analyse them as monomoraic single nuclei (pp. 17-18).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the section only describes primary stress and intonation.
new_statements.exceptions: Aspectual enclitics -eh and -am are excluded from stress assignment (p. 26); in compound nouns, phrases, idioms and serial verbs primary stress goes to the final syllable of the first word, not of the last word (pp. 26-29); apparent minimal pairs such as tabáŋ 'got killed' / ta-bá:ŋ 'ask us' / tá ba:ŋ 'ask to add' and bɛ́ hɛr 'dropped mangoes' vs bɛ́ hɛ́r 'mangoes dropped' are explained as word vs phrase vs clause, not lexical contrast (pp. 27-28).
new_statements.identity_note: Haan 2001 describes Adang as spoken in the villages west and northwest of Kalabahi (Adang-Buom, Kenarilang, O'a, Afeng, etc; pp. 4-5). Footnote 7 (p. 5) notes that Wurm & Voorhoeve treat Adang as a dialect of Kabola and Grimes et al. 1997 treat Adang as an alternative name for Kabola, but that "Adang speakers and Kabola speakers do not always understand each other", the difference being "especially in the area of phonology", whereas Adang and Hamap speakers always understand each other. The stress statement therefore applies to Adang proper (adan1251), not necessarily to Kabola (kabo1247), whose phonology Haan says has diverged.

sources.note: The only full grammar; its phonology chapter is the primary source for Adang stress (PHOIBLE, Sinnemäki & Ahola and Glottolog all rely on it). An open PDF exists at Sydney eScholarship but the host blocks our network (not reachable by automated download) and web.archive.org is unreachable from here; a 2024-12-19 Internet Archive copy of the record page exists. Needs a download from another network, or the MPG-internal LDH copy (PuRe item_401511, file_401510).

sources.citation: Holton, Gary & Laura C. Robinson. 2017. The internal history of the Alor-Pantar language family. In Marian Klamer (ed.), The Alor-Pantar languages: history and typology, 2nd ed., 49-90. Berlin: Language Science Press.
sources.note: Family-level transcription note only, p. 55 (p. 69): 'In most of the modern languages stress is on the penultimate syllable; however, stress may also be attracted to heavy syllables, as in Teiwa jiˈvar "dog". In addition, stress may be phonemically contrastive in some languages, as in Western Pantar baˈwa "conch shell" vs. ˈbawa "drum".' Adang is one of the twelve sampled languages but is not singled out; no Adang stress statement anywhere in the volume (a full-text search for stress/accent full text). Klamer's ch. 1 typological overview has no stress remark.
